summary: Defines a new attribute type and an auxiliary object class to store URIs, including URLs, in directory entries in a standard way.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC defines a directory attribute for storing a URI, such as a URL, with an optional label. It also defines an object class that lets directory entries use the attribute.

questions: how to store urls in an x.500 directory
how to store a url in an ldap entry
subtitle: Directory attributes for storing URIs with optional human-readable labels.

tldr.problem: Directory users needed a standard way to include URLs and other URIs in LDAP and X.500 entries.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the multivalued labeledURI attribute and an auxiliary labeledURIObject class that can be added to directory entries.
tldr.outcome: Directory entries can store URIs with optional labels; the earlier labeledURL attribute is deprecated.

today: RFC 2079 is a Proposed Standard. The unit metadata records no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Storing URIs in Directory Entries
sections.content: Groups had already experimented with storing URLs in LDAP and X.500 directories, but a standard form was needed. RFC 2079 defines the labeledURI attribute type and the auxiliary labeledURIObject class to hold URIs, including URLs. The definitions are designed for LDAP and X.500 directories and may be used in other contexts.
sections.plainLanguage: Directories needed a consistent way to store web addresses and other resource identifiers. This RFC defines an attribute and class for that purpose.

sections.title: The labeledURI Attribute
sections.content:
labeledURI uses case-exact string syntax and can have multiple values. A value consists of a URI, currently a URL, optionally followed by one or more spaces and a label. The RFC notes that spaces are not allowed unencoded inside a URI, so a space separates the URI from its label.

The label is a friendly name for people, and the RFC defines no required label syntax. It discourages non-ASCII label characters because directory clients may handle them differently. Multiple values can identify related resources or different locations for the same resource.
sections.plainLanguage: An entry can hold several URIs. Each one may have a plain-language label after it to help a person identify the resource.

sections.title: The labeledURIObject Class
sections.content:
The labeledURIObject class is an auxiliary class, a subclass of top, that may contain the labeledURI attribute. It can be added to existing directory objects, and the attribute may also be included directly in other object classes.

The appendix describes an earlier labeledURL attribute as deprecated. It should not be used for new values, though directory clients may support it to help sites transition away from it.
sections.plainLanguage: The class lets an existing directory entry carry labeled URIs. The earlier labeledURL attribute is deprecated and should not be used for new values.

sections.title: A Warning About Labels in HTML
sections.content: The RFC does not otherwise discuss security, but warns against blindly inserting the label portion of a labeledURI value into an HTML document. A malicious person could put HTML tags in a label and mislead people viewing the document.
sections.plainLanguage: Do not insert a label into a web page without handling it carefully. A label could contain HTML that misleads readers.
